questions.q: State the exact ionic distribution across the axonal membrane at rest and name the protein responsible for maintaining it.
questions.a: At rest, the axoplasm has high K⁺ and negatively charged proteins, low Na⁺; the extracellular fluid has high Na⁺, low K⁺. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump maintains this by actively transporting 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP hydrolysed. A wrong answer (e.g., "Na⁺ is high inside") reveals the student has not grasped the pump's directionality or the concept of electrochemical gradients.

questions.q: Explain why the rising phase of the action potential is extremely brief, even though Na⁺ channels remain open for a few milliseconds.
questions.a: The rising phase is brief because Na⁺ channels rapidly inactivate (not just close) within ~1 ms, and simultaneously voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, driving K⁺ efflux that counteracts Na⁺ influx. A student who says "Na⁺ channels close slowly" confuses inactivation with deactivation and misses the critical role of K⁺ efflux in terminating depolarisation.

questions.q: A neuron is treated with a toxin that irreversibly blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels. Predict the effect on the action potential waveform and the neuron's ability to fire repeatedly.
questions.a: Depolarisation (Na⁺ influx) will occur normally, but repolarisation will be severely delayed or absent because K⁺ efflux is blocked. The membrane will remain depolarised, inactivating Na⁺ channels and preventing subsequent action potentials — the neuron becomes inexcitable. A wrong prediction (e.g., "action potentials become faster") shows failure to link K⁺ efflux to both repolarisation and recovery from inactivation.

questions.q: Compare the energy demand (ATP consumption) of a myelinated axon versus an unmyelinated axon of the same length conducting the same number of action potentials.
questions.a: The myelinated axon consumes significantly less ATP because depolarisation (and thus Na⁺/K⁺ pump activity to restore gradients) occurs only at nodes of Ranvier, whereas in unmyelinated axons the entire membrane depolarises. A student who claims "myelinated axons use more ATP because they conduct faster" confuses conduction velocity with ionic flux per unit length.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since the Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, it directly creates the action potential by making the inside more negative." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The pump establishes the *concentration gradients* (resting potential), but the action potential is generated by *passive* ion fluxes through voltage-gated channels (Na⁺ in, then K⁺ out). The pump is too slow to drive the millisecond-scale voltage reversal. A student who agrees confuses the *setup* (gradient creation) with the *trigger* (channel gating).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a frog sciatic nerve preparation to demonstrate that nerve impulse conduction is an active, energy-dependent process (not simple electrical conduction like a wire).
questions.a: Stimulate the nerve and record compound action potentials. Then apply a metabolic inhibitor (e.g., cyanide) or remove oxygen/glucose. Conduction will fail within minutes as ATP depletes and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops, collapsing gradients. A wire would conduct indefinitely without metabolism. A poor design (e.g., only measuring speed) misses the key test: metabolic dependence.
